overview: The Ghaznavids built a major empire from Ghazni, linking Afghanistan, eastern Iran and northwestern India. Their dynasty lasted from 977 to 1186, with much smaller territories in its later years. The atlas instead repeats a broad outline from 1000 through 1279. That outline misses the empire’s contraction and continues after its end; it should not be read as a reliable frontier for every selected year.

periods.title: A dynasty forms
periods.summary: Sebuktegin established a ruling house at Ghazni.

periods.title: Expansion
periods.summary: Mahmud’s conquests created an extensive military empire.

periods.title: A smaller realm
periods.summary: Defeat in Khorasan shifted power toward Afghanistan and India.

periods.title: Lahore and conquest
periods.summary: The final rulers governed mainly in Punjab before the Ghurid conquest.

items.text: The dynasty grew out of the Samanid military system. Sebuktegin was formerly an enslaved soldier who rose to command at Ghazni. His son Mahmud then became an independent conqueror. One family’s extraordinary rise took place within a system that continued to enslave other people.

Mahmud’s large army needed continual funding. Taxes, seized temple treasures and captives taken during Indian campaigns helped sustain it. Court buildings and poetry belong in the same history as the costs imposed on taxpayers and conquered communities. Military success did not mean a comfortable life for everyone.

Running the empire also required skilled Persian secretaries and officials. They managed the administration behind the soldiers, while court poets competed for royal support. Ghaznavid power joined a Turkish ruling family, Persian administrative and literary traditions, and subjects of many backgrounds.

At Dandanqan in 1040, Seljuq forces defeated Masud I’s army, already weakened by famine and drought. Khorasan passed out of Ghaznavid control. Even a heavily equipped army could lose when food, water and mobility became decisive problems.

sections.title: Courtyards, crafts and the work of daily life

items.text: The excavated palace at Ghazni had a central courtyard with four large vaulted openings, or iwans. Rooms lay behind antechambers, a mosque served the complex, and private quarters occupied a smaller southwestern courtyard. Its plan separated public ceremony from more secluded household spaces; it describes a royal residence, not an ordinary family’s house.

Ghazni’s carved marble was originally painted and gilded. Craftspeople made leafy patterns, geometric designs and inscriptions, using stone available from a nearby quarry. The skills had local roots: researchers identify continuities with earlier Hindu-Shahi stoneworking. The city’s makers carried knowledge across changes of rulers.

Marble finds include basins, well surrounds, tanks and manhole covers as well as glamorous wall panels. Water needed practical fittings, too. These objects give archaeologists evidence of water systems, although they do not establish how clean every household’s supply was or whether everyone had a private toilet.

Studies of excavated pottery identify local production of both glazed and unglazed ceramics, especially during the eleventh to thirteenth centuries. Imported fine wares also reached Ghazni from Iraq, Iran, Central Asia and China. Potters’ workshops and long-distance exchange continued through the change from Ghaznavid to Ghurid rule.

The royal kitchen had its own department: sources use the title khwansalar for its supervisor and workers in the Ghaznavid period. Feeding a palace involved organized labour with recognized jobs. Someone still had to do the cooking, however magnificent the dining surroundings.

Streams supplied Ghazni, and rulers developed extensive gardens. Masud I moved among garden residences in several cities; his Balkh complex included a bazaar as well as buildings. These places combined royal display, business and the work needed to keep cultivated spaces alive.

The historian Bayhaqi first studied in Nishapur, then learned government work in Mahmud’s secretariat. For nineteen years he served under Abu Nasr Mushkan, preparing important letters and neat final copies. His education continued on the job, and that close view of court business later helped him write history.

Al-Biruni observed the sky from Ghazni between 1018 and 1020 to determine the city’s latitude. He also studied Sanskrit and translated Indian texts into Arabic. His work on India discussed marriage customs, religion, numbers and calendars, showing how careful language study could open a window onto another society.

Al-Biruni’s pharmacy book, Kitab al-Saydana, organized information about drugs alphabetically and recorded names in several languages. Different names could refer to the same substance, making identification an important scholarly problem. This was historical medical knowledge, assembled from earlier authors and observation, rather than a recipe book for modern home treatment.

Under the Ghaznavid ruler Bahramshah, Nasr-Allah Monshi produced a Persian version of Kalila wa Dimna, a collection of animal fables. He mixed Persian prose with Arabic verse. Talking animals carried lessons about human behaviour and political judgement, giving serious advice a much livelier cast of characters.

sections.title: A small piece of original writing

items.text: A silver dirham minted at Ghazni and catalogued to 1020 or 1021 carries “محمد رسول الله”, meaning “Muhammad is the messenger of God”. The same coin names Mahmud and the Abbasid caliph al-Qadir. On a disc less than two centimetres wide, Arabic writing connected money, religious belief and political authority.

ending.text: After losing Ghazni, the final Ghaznavids ruled mainly from Lahore. Ghurid forces captured that city in 1185 to 1186 and imprisoned Khusrow Malek and his son, ending the dynasty. People and literary traditions continued under new rulers; later writers preserved memories of Lahore’s poets. The imported 1279 cutoff is not the date of this conquest.
